Kiva United Energy, Inc. - Bakersfield 
EPA Identification Number 1000-0014-3472
----------
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

ES  1.0 FACILITY ACCIDENTAL RELEASE POLICY
The owners, management, and employees of Kiva United Energy, Inc. (Kiva)  Bakersfield (herein referred to as Bakersfield or Bakersfield Terminal) are committed to the prevention of accidental releases of odorized, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG, propane). Kiva has prepared this Risk Management Plan (RMP) in accordance with both the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA) and California Accidental Release Prevention (CalARP) Program regulations to address process and operational safety. 
.
If an accidental release were to occur, the Facility is prepared to work with the local fire department, or other authorities, to mitigate the release and to minimize the impact of the release on people and the environment. A detailed Emergency Response Program (ERP) has been developed and will be implemented in the event of an accidental release. 
.
----------
ES  2.0 FACILITY INFORMATION
Kiva is a wholesale distributor of propane. At the Bakersfield Terminal, the maximum amount of propane in inventory exceeds the U.S. EPA regulatory threshold of 10,000 lbs. The facility is required to prepare both a federal RMP as well as a California RMP.
	The Bakersfield Terminal has been assigned the U.S. EPA Facility Identifier number 
1000 0014 3472 and has a physical address of 4937 Standard Street, Bakersfield, California 93308. 

	The facility is assigned the NAICS code 42471, Petroleum Bulk Stations and Terminals. No Safer Technologies and Alternatives Analysis (STAA) is required .

	The terminal is a bulk, hydrocarbon storage and handling facility that receives LPG by rail cars and, to a lesser degree, trucks. 

	Rail service to the Terminals siding is provided by San Joaquin Valley Railroad. Cars are spotted on the two sidings that extend the length of the western property line.

	The sidings at the Bakersfield Terminal

have capacity for 19 tank cars.
 
	Propane is received at the terminal in US DOT tank cars (typically DOT 105, 112, or 114 ), with a shell volume of up to 33,700 gallons.

	The tank cars are spotted at towers, at which Terminal employees connect vapor and liquid lines located on the tank dome. 

	A compressor is used to create a pressure differential between the tank cars and the pressure vessels, which moves the liquefied, compressed gas into the storage tanks.

	Propane received via DOT transport trucks would be loaded into the storage vessels at one of the loading racks. The transport vehicles would be unloaded using a liquid pump.

	The liquefied petroleum gas is stored in the terminals 35 aboveground, pressure vessels (tanks). The 35 tanks are interconnected into seven groups of five vessels. See the table below. Each group of five pressure vessels operated as if it were a single storage vessel.

	Terminal employees oversee load-out operations of the propane into US DOT transports owned by Kiva as well as those owned by third-party distributors of propane. Kiva uses liquid pumps to load the US DOT approved LPG transport trucks of approximately 10,600 gallons or bobtail delivery trucks of approximately 3,000 gallons.

	The storage vessels are protected by an automatic fire protection system (a deluge system) that would activate and automatically initiate a response from the local fire department in the event of a fire within the tank yard.

	The maximum amount of propane present within the interconnected storage vessels is 4,870,846 lbs.

	The maximum amount of propane present within the DOT railcars on the Bakersfield Terminal sidings is 2,296,756 lbs. This value assumes that railcars spotted at the Terminal are of the nominal maximum size for the railcars. 

	The total mass of propane that could be in storage at the terminal, including the material in the tanks and in the railcars, is approximately 7.17 million pounds.

ES3.0	ACCIDENTAL RELEASE PREVENTION PROGRAM
The Facility has

implemented the following prevention program elements.
Process Safety Information. The Facility ensures that information concerning covered processes and regulated substances is up-to-date and available for review by employees. Safety Information includes a block flow diagram, Piping and Instrumentation Diagrams (P&IDs), Safety Data Sheets (SDSs), chemical inventories, operating limits (temperatures, pressures, flows, compositions), equipment specifications, and Codes and Standards used to design, build, and operate the process. The Program 3 items also include descriptions of safety systems, and materials of construction information for the installed systems. 
~~~~~
Process Hazards Analysis. A review of the process is conducted every five years or as needed following a process change. A review of the results from the most recent hazard review for the process indicate that no high-risk hazards were identified by the review team.
~~~~~
Operating Procedures. Written operating procedures have been developed for the covered processes. The operating procedures for the propane are reviewed and recertified on an annual basis.
 ~~~~~
Training. Terminal personnel and Kiva corporate management understand that incidents involving the accidental release of regulated substances can be reduced by having adequately trained operations and maintenance (O&M) personnel. A training program, which incorporates operating procedures and safe work practices, is an essential element of an effective prevention program. The current training program is comprised of the following:
	Initial employee training.
	Periodic refresher training.
	Training provided for new equipment additions or modifications.
	Competency testing involving written tests and observation following training; and
	Training records for each employee.
~~~~~
Mechanical Integrity. The Bakersfield Terminal has implemented a Mechanical Integrity program for its regulated substances. The program at the Facility is intended to

preserve the mechanical integrity of the process equipment to minimize the potential for an accidental release. The program includes equipment inspection, preventive maintenance, recordkeeping, and training and is conducted in accordance with manufacturers requirements and industry practices (e.g., Recognized and Generally Accepted Good Engineering Practices, RAGAGEP). 
~~~~~
Management Of Change. Operational, safety, and environmental issues must be reviewed prior to the initiation of a process change to ensure that they do not compromise the safety and integrity of the Process, and to minimize adverse effects on worker safety and public health. The Management of Change (MOC) procedures are used to evaluate changes to process materials, controls, equipment, and procedures.
~~~~~
Pre-Startup Safety Review. The pre-startup safety review (PSSR) applies to additions or modifications to the Process that require the safety information to be revised or updated. As changes in affected processes are identified or planned, they must be evaluated and a PSSR completed if deemed necessary in accordance with operating procedures. The assessment is undertaken in conjunction with the MOC review. A PSSR is performed in conjunction with the MOC review process when the proposed change requires modifications to the safety or operational procedures.
~~~~~
Compliance Audits. Kiva conducts triennial compliance audits of the RMP program to assess the effectiveness of the written plan and to identify gaps in the program. Records of the audits and follow-up documentation are maintained to indicate findings and resolution of findings. 
Incident Investigation. Although no incidents involving regulated substances have occurred at the Facility in the last five years, Kiva has an incident investigation program and documentation in place. The program includes investigation requirements and reporting and would be implemented in the event of an incident.

Other Code Applicability. The Facility implements the provisions of the following guidelines, regulations, and standards for these regulated substances (partial list):
	California Code of Regulations, Title 8, Division 1, Chapter 4, Subchapter 1, Unfired Pressure Vessel Safety Orders, Articles 2 and 6.
	California Code of Regulations, Title 19 [Public Safety], Division 5, [California Environmental Protection Agency], Chapter 1 [Hazardous Materials Inventory and Response Plans].
	California Code of Regulations, Title 19 [Public Safety], Division 5, [California EPA], Chapter 2 [California Accidental Release Prevention Program Detailed Analysis].
	United States Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), 29 CFR 1910.38, Employee emergency response plan and fire prevention plans. 
	United States Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA), 40 CFR Chapter I, Subchapter C, Part 68, Chemical Accident Prevention Provisions.
	United States Department of Labor, Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), 29 CFR 1910.110, Storage and Handling of Liquefied Petroleum Gases.
	National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 58  Liquefied Petroleum Gas Code. 
	NFPA 70  National Electrical Code.

ES4.0	FIVE-YEAR ACCIDENT HISTORY
There have been no accidental releases of propane during the last five years resulting in death, injuries, evacuations, shelter in-place orders, or property or environmental damage.

ES5.0	THE EMERGENCY RESPONSE PROGRAM
The Bakersfield Terminal maintains a written emergency procedure, which is in place to protect the workers and public safety as well as the environment. The procedures describe the manner of response to a fire or explosion if a flammable substance is accidentally released. The procedures address notification of local emergency response agencies if a release occurs. Employees receive training in emergency procedures. 

The Facility developed an Emergency Response

Program (ERP) in accordance with the requirements presented in the CalARP regulations Section 5120.2. The Emergency Response Program is developed in accordance with Title 19, Division 5, Chapter 1, Article 3, Section 5030.9 Emergency Response Plans and Procedures. The ERP will be implemented in the event of an accidental release of a regulated substance. 

The overall emergency procedure program for the Bakersfield Terminal is coordinated with local emergency responders in Kern County. This coordination involves periodic meetings of the committee, which include local emergency response officials, local government officials and industry representatives. The Bakersfield Terminal has around-the-clock communications capability with appropriate Emergency Management Program officials and emergency response organizations (e.g., Kern County Fire Department). This provides a means of notifying the public of an incident, if necessary, as well as facilitating quick response to an incident. The facilitys emergency response program is developed in accordance with Section 25503, Division 6.95 of the California Health and Safety Code, Hazardous Materials Business Plan requirements. 

ES6.0	PLANNED CHANGES TO IMPROVE SAFETY
Safety is integral to the operations at the Bakersfield Terminal. Implementing safety improvements is an on-going process at the Facility. Kiva conducts periodic evaluations to assess the effectiveness of the maintenance and safety programs. Specific changes to the propane process at the Facility will be implemented as needed.

ES7.0	THE WORST-CASE RELEASE AND ALTERNATIVE RELEASE SCENARIOS
The Bakersfield Terminal prepared offsite consequence analyses (OCA) for the propane process at the facility. The OCAs evaluated the Worst-Case Release Scenario (as defined in regulation) and an Alternative Release Scenario (i.e., the more likely condition). 
Worst Case Release Scenario. The worst-case release scenario is the failure of a set of five manifolded storage tan

ks when filled to the greatest amount. At the Bakersfield Terminal, Kiva has groups of five tanks, with a combined water volume of 200,000 gallons, filled to 85% volume. The mass of propane contained in the manifolded tanks is 717,400 lbs. The worst-case release scenario would result in a distance to the 1 psi over pressure (endpoint) of 0.7 miles. 
Alternative Release Scenario. The alternative release scenario based on the hazard review (or a more plausible potential incident) is a catastrophic release from a full-sized (10,600-gallon water capacity), tanker truck filled to 80%. This scenario assumes that the tanker leaks from the bottom mounted entry valve and that the entire contents of the truck are released into the atmosphere. The alternative release scenario would produce a pressure wave with an endpoint of 1 pound per square inch gauge over atmospheric pressure that would extend 0.2 miles.
